title: Atisha's cook
hookLine: a legend: Atisha kept a bad-tempered cook as a teacher of patience
last: HAS THE AIM GROWN ITS WINGS.

cards: Every kitchen has a temperature, and this one ran hot.

When Atisha traveled to Tibet, the story goes, he brought along an attendant from India who cooked for him, and this man was difficult: rude, quick to snap, grumbling at everyone, his teacher included.
The Tibetans who met him were puzzled. Why would a great master keep a man like that, when someone kinder could do the job? Atisha's answer, in the story, is still retold.

teach.b: In the legend, Atisha says the cook isn't a servant at all. He's a teacher, the one who teaches patience.
Some tellings add a smile: the Tibetans were so gentle that, without the cook, Atisha would have had nothing left to practice on. It's told with a wink, but it lands on something serious.
Shantideva's guide, the one we met two days ago, has a whole chapter on patience. There he argues that a person who harms you gives you something no friend can: the chance to practice patience.
Without someone difficult, patience has nothing to grow on.

teach.h: SHANTIDEVA: AN ENEMY IS A TREASURE.
teach.b: He even compares an enemy to a treasure that turns up in your own house, unearned.
Shantideva gives the argument; Atisha's cook puts it in a kitchen, with a face and a bad mood. It's one thing to agree that difficult people teach patience. It's another to keep one on the payroll.
What it doesn't mean: the story isn't telling anyone to stay in harm's way or accept abuse.
Buddhist teachers speak of patience alongside wisdom: seeing clearly what's happening, and refusing to add your own anger to it. The cook is grumpy, not dangerous.

Closer to home, there may be a cook somewhere nearby: a coworker, a neighbor, a relative at the holiday table. The legend asks a quiet question. What if that person is the lesson, and not the obstacle to it?

how: Tibetan teachers tell the story of Atisha's cook when teaching patience, alongside Shantideva's chapter on patience, and some practitioners deliberately treat difficult people as teachers in their daily mind training.

o: a cook Atisha sent home for being rude to guests
a grumpy attendant Atisha kept to learn patience
the monk who cooked for Tibet's first king

p: a treasure found in your house
no added anger, no staying in harm

s: the story of the cook is a legend people tell
it's told as a legend, often with a smile.
the story means you should stay with someone who abuses you
patience goes with wisdom; the cook is grumpy, not dangerous.
Shantideva says difficult people give you the chance to practice patience
it's in his chapter on patience.

games.q: you're Atisha. your cook is rude to everyone, including you. your Tibetan hosts offer to find someone kinder. what do you say?
o: no, he's my teacher of patience.
games.why: in the legend, Atisha keeps him, and calls him his teacher of patience.

practice: Bring to mind someone who rubs you the wrong way, not someone who has truly hurt you, and see their face, letting any tightness in the chest or jaw simply be there.
Then, on an out-breath, say inwardly a few times: thank you for the practice. You don't have to mean it fully yet.

wordCard.voice: Atisha's cook. In the legend, a bad-tempered attendant Atisha kept on purpose, calling him his teacher of patience. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit for patience, the subject of Shantideva's chapter: forbearance that doesn't add anger.

carryVoice: Your line: my teacher of patience. Grumpy, not dangerous, and still a teacher. Day nine hundred sixty-nine, in the books.
